reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease
clinicalPearls: A dominantly inherited disorder of sialic acid overproduction caused by activating (dominant-negative) variants in the allosteric site of GNE
Characterised by massive urinary excretion of free (unconjugated) N-acetylneuraminic acid, the sialic acid intermediate
It differs fundamentally from the sialic acid storage disorders, where the problem is lysosomal accumulation rather than cytoplasmic overproduction
Clinical features are variable and often relatively mild: coarse facies, hepatomegaly, recurrent infections, and variable developmental delay
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating grossly elevated free sialic acid in urine, distinguishing it from bound sialic acid disorders
The same GNE gene, when affected by different loss-of-function variants, causes GNE myopathy, illustrating gene-specific allelic diversity
There is no specific therapy; management is supportive with monitoring of growth and development
Prognosis is generally more favourable than for the severe sialic acid storage diseases
reference.pathophysiology: Sialuria is caused by variants that disrupt the allosteric feedback site of GNE, the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase that catalyses the rate-limiting steps of sialic acid biosynthesis. Normally the end-product, CMP-sialic acid, feeds back to inhibit this enzyme. When the regulatory site is disrupted, feedback inhibition is lost and the cytoplasm overproduces free N-acetylneuraminic acid, which is then excreted in large amounts in the urine and accumulates in tissues. This is distinct from the sialic acid storage disorders, in which a lysosomal transporter defect traps sialic acid within lysosomes. The overproduction phenotype tends to be milder, with variable somatic and developmental features.
additionalDifferentials: Sialic acid storage disorders (Salla disease, infantile free sialic acid storage disease)
Other lysosomal storage disorders with coarse facies and hepatomegaly
Other causes of hepatomegaly with developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary free sialic acid (markedly elevated)
Measurement of bound versus free sialic acid to distinguish storage disorders
Liver function tests and abdominal imaging for hepatomegaly
Metabolic screening to exclude alternative storage disorders
redFlags: Significant developmental regression prompting reassessment for an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Generally more benign than the sialic acid storage disorders, with variable outcome; many affected individuals have relatively mild disease, though developmental delay may occur.
pitfalls: Confusing sialuria (overproduction, free sialic acid excreted) with sialic acid storage disease (lysosomal accumulation)
Failing to distinguish free from bound sialic acid on testing
Assuming a severe storage-disease prognosis and counselling incorrectly
Overlooking the shared GNE gene basis with the distinct GNE myopathy
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Supportive, manifestation-directed care as no disease-specific therapy exists for the GNE overproduction defect
Early developmental intervention and educational support for variable developmental delay
Monitoring for and prompt treatment of recurrent infections
Monitoring of hepatomegaly with liver function tests and abdominal imaging
Coordinated multidisciplinary metabolic and developmental follow-up
Genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance, noting that variants often arise de novo
